newsitem.title: USA: Former president keeps tabs on Brazil from Miami.
newsitem.headline: Former president keeps tabs on Brazil from Miami.

text.p: Former President Fernando Collor de Mello, forced out of office by corruption charges in 1992, said he intended to continue playing a role in his country's politics despite his self-imposed exile in Miami.
But Collor said in an interview late on Monday that he had no immediate plans to seek elected office in Brazil.
"I have no motivation to run in an electoral contest. My motivation only exists in the field of ideas, of proposals and political debate," Collor told Reuters.

The former president, who is 47, has begun writing his memoirs, making public appearances and touting his political line on his homepage on the Internet (http://www.collor.com), inveighing against monopolies in Brazil and President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's stand on Indian rights.
Collor criticised Cardoso for seeking to reform Brazil's constitution to allow two consecutive presidential terms.
"With so many more important reforms pending, doesn't this have a purely personal or party motivation?" he asked.
Collor resigned in 1992, just hours before being impeached by Brazil's Senate in the midst of allegations of financial wrongdoings by his campaign treasurer, Paulo Cesar Farias.

A dashing figure who became Brazil's youngest president in 1989 promising to end corruption, Collor quit amid scandal and charges that he had benefited from a slush fund that funnelled millions of dollars to his family, friends and former aides.
Collor was later acquitted by Brazil's Supreme Court, but he remains barred from seeking public office until 2000. He left Brazil two years ago.

"It's really a self-exile because the process that took me away from the presidency of the republic was a long, hard and painful process," he said in his office in a high tower in Miami's financial district.
"Unfortunately the political persecution did not end at the time of my acquittal by the Federal Supreme Tribunal of the accusations made against me," he said.

Collor received additional scrutiny earlier this year when Farias and his mistress were found dead with bullet wounds, a case that has not been solved but which silenced a key witness in the corruption affair that ended Collor's presidency.
He said he was on vacation in Tahiti at the time.
